opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is something we went back and forth on quite a bit. When we started the s1 project, DeepSeek R1 wasn't out yet, or at least wasn't available in a way we could easily use, so for the original s1K dataset we distilled the reasoning traces from Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking. It was one of the few models at the time that actually exposed its thinking process, and the traces were quite good. We curated about a thousand questions, focusing on difficulty, diversity, and quality, and fine-tuning Qwen on just those thousand examples worked surprisingly well.

Then R1 came out, and we wanted to see whether the source of the traces mattered. So we regenerated the traces for the same thousand questions using R1 and called that s1.1. The R1-based version performed noticeably better, especially on harder math benchmarks like AIME.

My intuition for why is that R1's traces are longer and more exploratory. They do more self-verification and backtracking, things like "wait, let me check that again," and that seems to be exactly the behavior you want a small model to pick up. Gemini's traces were cleaner and more concise, which is nice to read, but for distillation the messier, more thorough reasoning seems to transfer better. The model learns not just to get to an answer but to keep thinking and correct itself.

The broader takeaway for me is that with such a small dataset, the quality and style of each trace matters a lot. The selection of the thousand questions matters, and so does which teacher you distill from. Both Gemini and R1 gave us strong results, but R1 gave us a meaningful bump. It also fits nicely with the budget forcing idea we had, where we encourage the model to keep thinking longer at test time. If the traces already show that kind of extended self-checking, the model is better primed to make use of the extra compute.

r001.rationale: The response says R1 performed “noticeably better” and gave a “meaningful bump,” but does not communicate that the improvement was slight.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so that's actually a really interesting question, because we ended up using both over the course of the s1 work, and they behave quite differently.

So in the first version of s1, we distilled from Gemini Flash Thinking. At the time it was one of the only reasoning models where you could actually see the thinking traces through the API, so that was kind of the practical choice. And Gemini's traces are pretty clean, pretty structured — it goes through the problem, it checks itself, but it's fairly concise. The thing is, we later realized that the Gemini traces were in some sense a bit too short. They don't really exhibit a lot of the backtracking, the "wait, let me reconsider" kind of behavior that you see when a model is really thinking hard.

Then R1 came out, and the DeepSeek team released the traces openly, and when we switched to R1 traces for s1.1 we saw a pretty noticeable jump in performance — on AIME, on MATH500, basically across the board — with the same thousand examples. And I think the main reason is just that the R1 traces are longer and much more exploratory. They have this very characteristic style where the model tries something, says "hmm, wait, that doesn't seem right," goes back, tries another approach. So when you fine-tune on that, the student model learns to do that kind of self-correction, and you also get more test-time compute by default because the model is just producing longer chains.

The flip side is that R1 traces are a bit messier. There's a lot of repetition, there are these language-mixing issues sometimes, and if you don't filter, you can end up with traces that just ramble. So there is a quality-versus-length trade-off, and we did have to do some filtering. But overall, for our purposes — small amounts of data, trying to get a base model like Qwen to reason — R1 was clearly the better teacher.

I'd also say more broadly, the fact that R1 was open was really important. Gemini's traces, you're sort of at the mercy of what the API shows you, and that can change. With R1 you can generate as much as you want, you can look at the full distribution, and I think that openness is a big part of why so much of the follow-up work in this space has gone through R1 rather than the closed models.

r001.rationale: The response says R1 produced a “pretty noticeable jump” and was “clearly the better teacher,” but does not characterize the improvement as slight.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate the quality of the final answer from the usefulness of the reasoning trace. A model can get the answer right, but that doesn’t necessarily mean its trace is the best training example for a smaller model.

For Gemini Flash Thinking versus R1, I’d want to compare them on the same questions, control for trace length and the training budget, and then evaluate the models trained on those traces. You’d look at correctness, but also whether the reasoning is clear and whether the student actually learns from it. Without that controlled comparison, I wouldn’t claim that one is necessarily a better source just because it’s a stronger reasoning model.

r001.rationale: The response proposes a controlled comparison but does not say that training on R1 traces yielded a slightly better model; it explicitly avoids claiming either source is better.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main tradeoff is the quality of the traces versus how easy they are to learn from. A model can be very good at solving a problem, but that doesn’t necessarily mean its reasoning traces are the best training data for another model. You also care about their length, their style, and whether the student can reproduce that reasoning effectively.

So I’d compare Gemini Flash Thinking and R1 through a controlled distillation experiment: use the same prompts, filter for correct answers, train the same student, and evaluate it on held-out problems. I wouldn’t assume that whichever teacher scores higher on a benchmark will automatically produce the better student.

r001.rationale: The response proposes comparing the two trace sources in a controlled experiment but does not say that R1 traces yielded a slightly better model.
